lessons.title: Seasonal campaigns and the retail calendar
lessons.body:
### Seasons drive e-commerce

Demand in e-commerce rises and falls with seasons, holidays and cultural events. Planning ahead lets you secure stock, prepare creative, book creators and ads, and avoid last-minute discounting.

### A global and regional retail calendar (examples)

| Period | Events | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| January | New Year sales, "new year, new me" | Fitness, organisation, self-improvement |
| Varies (lunar calendar) | Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr | Major season in the Gulf, Pakistan and Muslim communities worldwide; shopping patterns shift (late-night browsing), gifting and clothing peaks before Eid |
| Varies (lunar calendar) | Eid al-Adha | Travel, clothing, food and gifting |
| February | Valentine's Day (in markets where it is marketed) | Gifting |
| March–May | Mother's Day (dates vary by country), spring launches | Check dates per market |
| Summer | Summer sales, travel, back to school (timing varies) | School calendars differ by country |
| Varies | Diwali | Major gifting season in South Asian markets and diaspora |
| 11 November | Singles' Day / 11.11 | Big in parts of Asia and adopted by some marketplaces elsewhere |
| Late November | Black Friday / White Friday, Cyber Monday | White Friday is the name used by some Gulf retailers and marketplaces |
| December | Christmas, Boxing Day, year-end | Gifting and clearance in many markets |
| Local | National days, regional festivals, pay days | E.g. UAE National Day, Saudi National Day, Pakistan's Independence Day |

Because Islamic calendar dates move roughly 10–11 days earlier each Gregorian year, Ramadan and Eid planning must be updated annually.

### The campaign planning timeline

```
T-12 to T-8 weeks: Decide objectives, products, offers; check stock and supplier lead times
T-8 to T-6 weeks:  Brief creative; book creators; plan email/SMS calendar; landing pages
T-6 to T-4 weeks:  Build audiences; warm-up content; grow email/SMS list (early access)
T-4 to T-1 weeks:  Teasers; QA site speed, checkout, codes, tracking; customer service prep
Campaign period:   Launch; monitor daily (stock, conversion, ad performance, site health)
T+1 to T+2 weeks:  Post-campaign flows (thank you, cross-sell, reviews); analysis and learnings
```

### Operations are marketing

Peak seasons stress operations. Coordinate with logistics and customer service:

- Stock levels for hero products.
- Courier capacity and cut-off dates (especially before Eid or Christmas).
- Clear "order by" dates on the site.
- Extra customer service coverage, including messaging channels.
- Returns policy communication for gifts.

### Campaign messaging

- Lead with the customer's occasion ("Eid outfits for the whole family"), not just discounts.
- Use genuine urgency (delivery cut-offs, limited stock) — clearly and truthfully.
- Create gift guides by recipient and budget.
- Respect cultural sensitivities: for Ramadan, tone and timing matter (for example, content suited to evening browsing hours and reflective themes rather than purely transactional messaging).

### Worked example: a Pakistani fashion brand's Eid plan

```
10 weeks before: Finalise Eid collection; order fabric; plan hero products
8 weeks:         Photoshoot; brief creators (with disclosure requirements); build landing page
6 weeks:         Launch waitlist and early-access sign-ups via Instagram and WhatsApp
3 weeks:         Collection reveal; email/SMS/WhatsApp campaigns to consented subscribers
2 weeks:         Paid social scaling; "order by" dates for delivery before Eid by city
Final week:      Delivery cut-off reminders; switch to "gift cards" and "Eid day 2" messaging
After Eid:       Thank-you flow; review requests; clearance of remaining stock
```

### Key dates for the 2026–27 season (check locally)

| Moment | Timing | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Saudi National Day | 23 September | Big promotional moment in KSA |
| Daraz 11.11 / 12.12 | 11 November / 12 December | Major marketplace sales in Pakistan and other Daraz markets |
| Black Friday / Cyber Monday | 27 and 30 November 2026 | UK, US and increasingly global; "White Friday" branding common in the Gulf, often spanning weeks |
| UAE National Day (Eid Al Etihad) | 2 December | Promotions around 1–3 December |
| Christmas / Boxing Day | 25–26 December | UK/US; delivery cut-offs matter |
| Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr | Expected to begin in early February 2027 (dates depend on moon sighting) | Ramadan moves about 11 days earlier each year; evening and late-night shopping peaks |
| Eid al-Adha | Expected mid-May 2027 | Gifting, fashion, travel |

Always confirm official dates and announcements, and plan delivery cut-offs with your couriers.

### Hands-on: a campaign timeline you can copy

```
T-8 weeks  Plan: goals, offers (with margin maths), hero products, stock orders, creative briefs
T-6 weeks  Feeds: seasonal custom labels, sale price dates, Merchant Center promotions submitted
T-4 weeks  Creative produced; landing pages built; email/SMS/WhatsApp flows drafted; marketplace deals registered
T-2 weeks  QA: pages, codes, feeds, tracking; courier cut-offs published; CS scripts and staffing
T-1 week   Warm-up: waitlists, early access for subscribers/members, teaser content
Live       Daily stand-up: sales, stock, ad pacing, site speed, CS queue; stop/adjust rules pre-agreed
T+1 week   Post-purchase flows; returns readiness; review requests timed after delivery
T+3 weeks  Retrospective: contribution margin, new-customer share, returns, what to repeat
```

### Using AI in seasonal planning

AI assistants help draft calendars, creative variations and localised copy (Arabic, Urdu, English) quickly. Check religious and cultural references with native speakers, verify dates against official sources, and never let generated copy promise delivery before a date your couriers cannot guarantee.

### Common mistakes

- Starting creative and stock planning too late.
- Discount-only messaging that ignores the occasion.
- Missing courier cut-off communication.
- Not testing the site under peak load.
- Forgetting post-campaign flows, when newly acquired customers are most receptive.

### Learning from each season

After every major event, hold a short retrospective with marketing, operations and customer service. Record what sold out, what was overstocked, which messages and creatives performed, where the site or checkout struggled, how many customer service contacts arrived and why, and how the new customers behaved in the weeks that followed. Store these notes with next year's calendar so the next campaign starts from evidence, not memory.

### Seasonal planning checklist

- [ ] Annual calendar with market-specific dates (update lunar dates yearly)
- [ ] Timeline working back from each key event
- [ ] Stock, courier and customer service plans aligned
- [ ] Creative and creators booked early
- [ ] Post-campaign retention flows ready
keyTakeaways: Seasonal peaks require planning 8–12 weeks ahead.
Retail calendars differ by market; lunar-calendar events shift each year.
Operations — stock, couriers, service — are part of campaign success.
Lead with the customer's occasion and use only genuine urgency.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why must Ramadan and Eid campaign dates be updated every year?
options: The Islamic calendar is lunar, so dates move about 10–11 days earlier each Gregorian year
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Lunar dates shift relative to the Gregorian calendar.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which is an example of genuine urgency for a seasonal campaign?
options: Clear courier cut-off dates for delivery before Eid
'Last chance' every day for a month
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Real delivery deadlines are truthful and useful.

knowledgeCheck.question: What should happen immediately after a seasonal campaign?
options: Post-campaign flows such as thank-yous, review requests and cross-sells, plus analysis
knowledgeCheck.explanation: New customers are receptive after purchase, and learnings improve the next campaign.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why can't you reuse last year's Ramadan campaign dates?
options: Ramadan follows the lunar calendar and moves about 11 days earlier each year, with dates confirmed by moon sighting
Ramadan dates are set by retailers
Ramadan is not relevant to ecommerce
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The Islamic calendar is lunar, so Ramadan shifts about 11 days earlier each Gregorian year. Plans must be rebuilt around the new dates and delivery cut-offs.

scenes.narration: In ecommerce, a few weeks can make or break the year. Ramadan and Eid in the Gulf and Pakistan. White Friday and Black Friday. Daraz eleven eleven. Christmas in the UK. Each moment brings a surge of demand, and a surge of competition for attention, stock and couriers. In this lecture you'll learn the regional retail calendar for the coming season, an eight-week planning timeline, why operations are marketing, how to shape campaign messaging, and how to learn from each season. Then you'll watch me build a campaign timeline backwards from a delivery cut-off.

scenes.narration: Why plan seasons so carefully? Because demand is concentrated, and so is competition. Ad costs usually rise in peak weeks. Couriers get busy, so delivery promises get harder to keep. Stock that runs out can't be replaced in time. And shoppers make decisions earlier than you'd think, often researching and wish-listing weeks before the big day. The brands that win peaks start early, plan capacity, and keep their promises.

• Stock can't be replaced in time
• Shoppers decide early

scenes.narration: Here's the calendar for the coming season. Saudi National Day on the twenty-third of September. Daraz eleven eleven on the eleventh of November and twelve twelve on the twelfth of December. Black Friday on the twenty-seventh of November twenty twenty-six and Cyber Monday on the thirtieth, with White Friday branding common in the Gulf, often running for weeks. UAE National Day on the second of December. Christmas and Boxing Day. Then Ramadan, expected to begin in early February twenty twenty-seven, depending on moon sighting, followed by Eid al-Fitr, and Eid al-Adha expected in mid-May. Always confirm official dates.

scenes.narration: Ramadan deserves special attention. It moves about eleven days earlier each year, so last year's plan needs shifting. Shopping patterns change: browsing and buying often peak in the evening after iftar and late at night. Gifting and fashion build towards Eid, with delivery cut-offs becoming the real deadline. And the tone matters. Messaging should respect the spirit of the month, focus on family, generosity and preparation, and avoid anything that feels careless about fasting or worship.

• Evening and late-night peaks

Six weeks: update product feeds with seasonal labels and sale dates, and submit promotions. Four weeks: creative produced, landing pages built, email, SMS and WhatsApp flows drafted, marketplace deals registered. Two weeks: QA everything and publish courier cut-offs. One week: warm-up and early access. Then live, with daily stand-ups. And afterwards: post-purchase flows, returns readiness and a retrospective.

scenes.narration: Operations are marketing. The best campaign fails if stock runs out, the site slows down, couriers miss dates or customer service can't answer. So plan stock by hero product, check site speed under load, agree capacity with couriers, publish delivery cut-offs clearly, staff customer service for the peak and prepare answers to the top questions. A promise kept at peak season earns loyalty. A promise broken earns one-star reviews.

scenes.narration: A simple example. A Pakistani fashion brand plans its Eid collection. Last year, they launched ten days before Eid and sold out of popular sizes, while late orders arrived after Eid, causing refunds and angry reviews. This year, they launch pre-orders five weeks out, publish a clear order-by date for delivery before Eid in each city, increase stock of the most requested sizes based on last year's data, and add WhatsApp order confirmations to reduce cash-on-delivery refusals. Same demand, far fewer broken promises.

Six weeks out, they add seasonal custom labels to their product feed, so Shopping campaigns can prioritise gift sets. They register marketplace deals and schedule sale prices with effective dates in the feed, so prices switch automatically and match the site. They publish Christmas delivery cut-offs agreed with their courier, and put them on every product page. They also plan a stop rule: if a hero product's stock falls below a set level, ads for it pause automatically. After the season, the retrospective shows which gift sets drove new customers who later bought again.

scenes.narration: Watch me build a timeline backwards. I start with the one date that matters most: the courier's last delivery date before Eid for the furthest city we serve. Say that's four days before Eid. So our order-by date is four days before Eid, and that goes on every page and in every message. Two weeks before that, QA: pages, codes, feeds and tracking, plus customer service scripts. Four weeks before, creative, landing pages and flows. Six weeks before, feed updates and promotion submissions. Eight weeks before, offers with margin maths, stock orders and briefs. Every task has an owner and a date. Working backwards from the promise makes the plan realistic.

scenes.narration: Your product feed and marketplaces need seasonal preparation too. In your Google Merchant Center feed, add a custom label for seasonal products, like eid twenty twenty-seven or gift sets, so campaigns can prioritise them. Schedule sale prices with effective dates, so prices switch automatically and match the site at exactly the right time. Submit promotions early enough for review. On marketplaces, register for deal events before their deadlines, check the reference-price rules, and plan stock for fulfilment centres, which often have inbound cut-offs weeks before the event. A beautiful campaign that isn't reflected in feeds and marketplace listings misses a large share of shoppers.

scenes.narration: Campaign messaging. Lead with the moment and the customer's goal: gifts that arrive before Eid, a wardrobe ready for the wedding season, presents sorted before the last Christmas post. Be specific about offers, deadlines and delivery. Localise properly: Arabic and Urdu copy written or reviewed by native speakers, not machine-translated and forgotten. AI can help draft calendars and variations quickly, but verify dates against official sources, and never let generated copy promise delivery your couriers can't guarantee.

Look at new-customer share and whether those customers buy again. Look at returns and refunds by product. Look at stock-outs, delivery performance and customer-service volume. And write down three things to repeat and three things to change, then put next year's key dates in the calendar right away.

modules.title: Retention, lifecycle marketing and loyalty
modules.summary: Turn first-time buyers into repeat customers with lifecycle flows, loyalty programmes and excellent customer experience.

lessons.title: Lifecycle email, SMS and messaging flows
lessons.body:
### Why retention matters so much

Acquiring a new customer usually costs more than keeping an existing one, and repeat customers often spend more over time. Retention marketing turns one-off buyers into repeat customers through timely, relevant communication.

### Owned channels

| Channel | Strengths | Considerations |
|---|---|---|
| Email | Rich content, low cost per message, automation | Deliverability, consent, inbox competition |
| SMS | High visibility, short and urgent messages | Cost per message, stricter consent rules in many countries, frequency sensitivity |
| Messaging apps (e.g. WhatsApp Business) | Conversational, popular in many markets including the Gulf and South Asia | Platform rules, opt-in requirements, template approval for business-initiated messages |
| Push notifications (app) | Instant for app users | Requires an app and permission |

### Core automated flows

```
1. WELCOME SERIES (new subscribers)
   - Deliver sign-up incentive (if any); brand story; bestsellers; social proof
2. BROWSE ABANDONMENT (viewed products, no cart)
   - Gentle reminder of viewed items; helpful content
3. CART ABANDONMENT
   - Reminder within hours; answer objections (delivery, returns); optional incentive later
4. CHECKOUT ABANDONMENT
   - Similar, focused on completing payment; alternative payment options
5. POST-PURCHASE
   - Order confirmation; shipping updates; how to use; review request; cross-sell
6. REPLENISHMENT
   - For consumables: reminder when the product is likely running out
7. WIN-BACK
   - For lapsed customers: what's new, incentive, feedback request
8. VIP / LOYALTY
   - Early access, exclusive offers, thank-you notes for top customers
```

Start with welcome, cart abandonment and post-purchase flows — they typically deliver the most value for the effort.

### Timing and content principles

- **Relevance beats frequency**: segment by behaviour (browsed categories, purchase history).
- **Lead with value**: helpful content, not just discounts. Reserve incentives for where they are needed.
- **Mobile-first design**: short copy, clear buttons.
- **One goal per message**.
- **Respect quiet hours** and cultural timing (for example, evening engagement during Ramadan).

### Consent and compliance

Rules vary by country and channel, but common principles apply:

- Get clear, informed consent for marketing messages where required (for example, under GDPR and PECR in the UK and EU; SMS rules such as the TCPA in the US are strict about consent).
- Keep proof of consent.
- Include an easy opt-out in every marketing message and honour it promptly.
- Separate **transactional** messages (order confirmations, shipping updates) from **marketing** messages.
- Messaging platforms have their own policies on business messaging and opt-in; follow them to avoid restrictions.

### Worked example: a UK coffee subscription brand

```
Welcome (3 emails):   Brewing guide; roaster story; bestseller trio
Post-purchase:        Brew tips for the beans purchased; review request after 10 days
Replenishment:        Reminder around the typical time a bag runs out (based on bag size)
Win-back:             After 60 days of no purchase - "new seasonal roast" + feedback survey
VIP:                  Early access to limited roasts for top customers
```

The brand monitors revenue per recipient, unsubscribe rate and repeat purchase rate.

### Collecting subscribers

- Pop-ups and embedded forms with a clear value (early access, guides, first-order offer).
- Checkout opt-in (unticked where required).
- Messaging opt-ins via click-to-chat buttons.
- Quizzes and product finders.
- Offline events and packaging inserts (with QR codes).

### Measuring lifecycle marketing

- Revenue per recipient and per flow.
- Conversion rate by flow.
- Repeat purchase rate and time between orders.
- List growth rate and unsubscribe/complaint rates.
- Deliverability (inbox placement, bounce rates).

Be cautious about attribution: some revenue attributed to emails would have happened anyway. Holdout tests (suppressing a flow for a small group) can estimate true incremental impact.

### Hands-on: specify your flows before you build them

Write each flow as a short spec your team (or agency) can build in any tool — Klaviyo, Omnisend, Mailchimp, Brevo, Shopify Email, or SMS tools such as Attentive and Postscript — and review for consent and exits:

```yaml
flow: cart_abandonment
trigger: started_checkout OR added_to_cart, no purchase within 1h
consent_required: email_marketing (email steps), sms_marketing (SMS step)
exit_when: placed_order OR unsubscribed
steps:
  - wait: 1h
    channel: email
    subject: "Your {{ first_item_name }} is still in your bag"
    content: item image, price, delivery date estimate, returns summary, CTA "Return to my bag"
  - wait: 20h
    channel: sms            # only if sms consent; respect quiet hours in the customer's time zone
    text: "{{brand}}: your bag is saved. Delivery by {{delivery_date}}. {{short_link}} Reply STOP to opt out"
  - wait: 48h
    channel: email
    subject: "Questions about {{ first_item_name }}?"
    content: top 3 FAQs for the category, reviews incl. one balanced, CTA; NO automatic discount
metrics: revenue per recipient, placed order rate, unsubscribe rate, spam complaint rate, SMS opt-out rate
holdout: 10% of eligible customers receive no flow (measures incremental revenue)
```

### WhatsApp and messaging in 2026

In the Gulf and South Asia, WhatsApp is often the most responsive channel. Business-initiated messages go through the **WhatsApp Business Platform** (via Meta or a solution partner) using **pre-approved templates**, with categories such as marketing, utility (order updates) and authentication, each priced differently by Meta. Rules to follow:

- Collect a clear **opt-in** that names WhatsApp before sending marketing templates.
- Use **utility** templates for order and delivery updates; keep marketing separate.
- Honour opt-outs immediately; low-quality or blocked messages can restrict your number.
- Check Meta's current pricing and policy pages — both change.

### Deliverability and SMS law, briefly

- Email: Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft require bulk senders to authenticate (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), support one-click unsubscribe and keep spam complaints low.
- SMS in the US: the TCPA requires prior express written consent for marketing texts; follow carrier registration rules for business numbers (e.g. 10DLC). UK/EU: PECR/ePrivacy consent rules, with a soft opt-in for existing customers in some cases.

### Holdouts for lifecycle marketing

Flows get credit for many orders that would have happened anyway. A **holdout** (a random 5–10% of eligible customers who do not receive the flow) shows the real incremental revenue — and often reveals that discounts in abandonment flows are unnecessary.

### Common mistakes

- Only sending promotional blasts.
- Discount in every message, training customers to wait.
- Sending marketing without consent.
- Ignoring post-purchase experience.
- Measuring email by opens alone (privacy features make open tracking unreliable).
- Sending the same message to every subscriber regardless of what they bought or browsed.
- Forgetting to suppress recent purchasers from promotions for the product they just bought.

### Lifecycle checklist

- [ ] Welcome, cart abandonment and post-purchase flows live
- [ ] Consent captured and recorded per channel
- [ ] Segmentation by behaviour
- [ ] Incremental impact estimated with holdouts where possible
- [ ] Monthly review of flow performance

lessons.title: Loyalty programmes, subscriptions and referrals
lessons.body:
### Building reasons to return

Beyond messages, you can build structural reasons for customers to come back: loyalty programmes, subscriptions, memberships and referral schemes.

### Types of loyalty programmes

| Type | How it works | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Points | Earn points per purchase; redeem for rewards | Frequent, moderate-value purchases |
| Tiered / VIP | Higher tiers unlock better benefits | Brands with a wide spread of customer value |
| Paid membership | Customers pay for benefits (e.g. free shipping, discounts) | High-frequency categories |
| Value-based / community | Access, content, events, causes | Lifestyle brands with strong identity |
| Cashback / wallet | Store credit on purchases | Price-sensitive markets |

### Designing a sustainable programme

1. **Define the goal**: more frequent purchases? Higher AOV? Better retention of top customers?
2. **Understand your economics**: what is the cost of rewards as a percentage of revenue? What behaviour change must happen to make it profitable?
3. **Make it simple**: customers should understand how to earn and redeem in one sentence.
4. **Offer meaningful rewards**: a mix of financial (discounts, credit) and experiential (early access, exclusive products, events).
5. **Communicate**: show point balances in emails, account pages and checkout.
6. **Manage liability**: unredeemed points can represent a financial liability; set clear terms and expiry in line with local law.

### Subscriptions

Subscriptions (replenishment of consumables like coffee, pet food, skincare) can create predictable revenue. Best practices:

- Flexible frequency, easy skip and pause options.
- Clear pricing and renewal terms before sign-up.
- **Easy cancellation** — regulators in many markets (for example, under UK consumer law reforms and US state automatic-renewal laws) scrutinise subscriptions that are hard to cancel or have unclear renewal terms.
- Reminders before renewal where required.

### Referral programmes

Satisfied customers can bring new ones. A typical structure: "Give 10%, get 10%" — the new customer gets a discount, the referrer gets credit after the friend's first order. Tips:

- Ask at moments of delight (after delivery, after a positive review).
- Make sharing easy (links for messaging apps and social).
- Prevent abuse (self-referrals, fake accounts) with rules and checks.
- Disclose incentives where referrers post publicly, as advertising rules may treat incentivised recommendations as endorsements.

### Measuring loyalty impact

Compare members and non-members carefully: members are often already your best customers (selection bias). Better methods:

- Compare behaviour before and after joining for similar customers.
- Use holdout groups when launching new benefits.
- Track repeat purchase rate, purchase frequency, AOV and retention by cohort.
- Track programme cost (rewards redeemed, admin, technology) against incremental margin.

### Worked example: a Saudi pet supplies store

The store sells pet food (frequent, predictable purchases) and accessories. It launches:

- **Subscription** for pet food with flexible delivery every 2, 4 or 6 weeks, easy skip, and a small saving versus one-off orders.
- **Points programme**: points on all purchases, bonus points on accessories (higher margin).
- **Referral**: "Give SAR 30, get SAR 30" after the friend's first order.

After six months, the team compares cohorts and finds subscribers order more often and churn less — while monitoring whether the subscription discount is paid back by the extra orders (outcome illustrative).

### Hands-on: is a referral reward affordable?

Before launching "give 20, get 20", check the maths with your own numbers (illustrative):

```python
def referral_economics(aov: float, gross_margin: float, variable_cost_per_order: float,
                       friend_reward: float, referrer_reward: float,
                       friend_repeat_orders_12m: float) -> dict:
    """Contribution from a referred customer over 12 months, after both rewards."""
    per_order = aov * gross_margin - variable_cost_per_order
    first_order = per_order - friend_reward - referrer_reward
    total_12m = first_order + per_order * friend_repeat_orders_12m
    return {"contribution_first_order": round(first_order, 2), "contribution_12m": round(total_12m, 2)}

print(referral_economics(aov=180, gross_margin=0.55, variable_cost_per_order=25,
                         friend_reward=20, referrer_reward=20, friend_repeat_orders_12m=1.2))
```

Compare the 12-month contribution with what you pay to acquire a customer through ads. If referred customers are cheaper and similarly loyal, referrals deserve more investment; if the first order loses money and repeat rates are low, reduce rewards or use non-cash rewards (early access, free delivery, gifts).

### Tools and 2026 practice

- **Loyalty apps** (for example Smile.io, LoyaltyLion, Yotpo Loyalty, Rivo) and **subscription apps** (Shopify Subscriptions, Recharge, Skio, Loop) integrate with major platforms; check local payment support for recurring billing in your market.
- **Wallet passes** and **WhatsApp** messages increasingly carry loyalty status in the Gulf and South Asia.
- **Subscription rules**: show renewal price and frequency next to the sign-up button, send reminders before renewals where required, and make cancellation easy online (US ROSCA and state laws; UK DMCC subscription rules being phased in; EU consumer rules).
- **Fraud controls** for referrals: one reward per new customer, reward after the friend's order passes the return window, and block self-referrals.

### Before and after: a loyalty programme pitch

```
BEFORE  "Join our rewards club and earn points!"
AFTER   "Members get free delivery on every order, early access to Eid drops, and 1 point per AED 1
         — 500 points = AED 25 off. Join free in 10 seconds."
```
The "after" leads with benefits customers value immediately and makes the points maths transparent.

### Common mistakes

- Programmes too complex to understand.
- Rewards that cost more than the behaviour change is worth.
- Hard-to-cancel subscriptions.
- Measuring loyalty impact without accounting for selection bias.
- Launching and never promoting the programme.

### Launching and promoting the programme

A programme nobody knows about changes nothing. Promote it on product pages, in the cart, at checkout, in post-purchase emails and on packaging inserts. Show customers what they would earn on the current order ("You'll earn 120 points with this purchase"). Remind members of their balance and upcoming expiry in lifecycle messages. Review membership sign-up rate, redemption rate and the behaviour of members against a fair comparison group each quarter, and simplify rules that customers find confusing.

### When not to launch a loyalty programme

If products are bought rarely (for example, furniture or mattresses), a points scheme may add cost without changing behaviour. In those categories, referral programmes, excellent service and post-purchase content often work better.

### Loyalty checklist

- [ ] Clear goal and economic model
- [ ] Simple earn and redeem rules
- [ ] Transparent terms, expiry and cancellation
- [ ] Referral abuse prevention
- [ ] Impact measured against a fair comparison
keyTakeaways: Loyalty programmes, subscriptions and referrals create structural reasons to return.
Design programmes around a clear goal and sustainable economics.
Subscriptions must have transparent terms and easy cancellation.
Measure loyalty impact while accounting for selection bias.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why can comparing loyalty members with non-members overstate the programme's impact?
options: Members are often already the best customers, so differences may not be caused by the programme
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Selection bias means members may have been loyal anyway.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is a key compliance consideration for subscription products?
options: Clear renewal terms and easy cancellation
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Regulators scrutinise subscriptions that are hard to cancel or unclear.

knowledgeCheck.question: When is the best moment to ask for a referral?
options: At moments of delight, such as after a successful delivery or positive review
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Satisfied customers are most likely to refer.

knowledgeCheck.question: Loyalty members spend three times more than non-members. Why doesn't this prove the programme works?
options: Because loyal, high-spending customers are more likely to join — selection bias; use holdouts or before/after cohorts instead
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Members self-select. Incremental impact needs a fair comparison such as a randomised holdout or cohort analysis.

scenes.narration: Every store wants loyal customers. Few stores ask the more useful question: why would anyone come back? Points and badges don't create loyalty on their own. Good products, great experiences and genuine reasons to return do. In this lecture you'll learn the types of loyalty programmes, how to design one that pays for itself, when subscriptions make sense and the rules that now govern them, how to run referral programmes that don't lose money, and how to measure what loyalty really adds. Then you'll watch me check whether a referral reward is affordable.

scenes.narration: Why invest in loyalty? Because repeat customers carry no acquisition cost for their later orders, often spend more over time, and refer friends. A small improvement in repeat rate can change the economics of the whole business. But loyalty programmes also cost money: rewards, software and management. A programme that mainly rewards people who would have come back anyway is just a discount with extra steps. So design for incremental behaviour.

Why loyalty matters
• Repeat orders skip acquisition cost
• Loyal customers refer others
• But programmes cost money
• Design for incremental behaviour

scenes.narration: Types of programmes. Points: earn per purchase, redeem for rewards; simple, but easy to ignore. Tiers: silver, gold and so on, with better benefits for higher spend; motivating for top customers. Paid memberships: pay a fee for ongoing benefits like free delivery. Value-based programmes: rewards like donations or community access. And subscriptions: regular deliveries of consumables. Think of it like a gym. Some people want pay-as-you-go, some want a membership, and some just want a friend to train with. Pick the model that fits your customers and your margins.
scenes.onScreen:
Programme types
• Points
• Tiers
• Paid membership
• Value-based; subscriptions
scenes.visual: Layout: five cards with icons (coin, podium, membership card, heart, repeat arrow) flip over as named; a gym analogy illustration sits alongside. Timing (39s): title 0-3s; 4 bullets build in narration order about every 8s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Designing a sustainable programme. Lead with benefits customers value immediately, like free delivery or early access, not just points in the distant future. Make the maths transparent: earn one point per dirham, five hundred points equals twenty-five dirhams off. Budget rewards as a percentage of revenue, and model the cost. Reward behaviours that help the business, like reviews, referrals, profile completion and app downloads, not just spend. And keep it simple enough to explain in one sentence.
scenes.onScreen:
Sustainable design
• Immediate, valued benefits
• Transparent points maths
• Budgeted reward cost
• Reward helpful behaviours; keep it simple
scenes.visual: Layout: a before/after pitch card: 'Earn points!' becomes 'Free delivery, early Eid access, 1 point per AED 1; 500 points = AED 25'; a small cost model chart appears beside it. Timing (33s): title 0-3s; 4 bullets build in narration order about every 6s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Subscriptions suit consumables and replenishment: coffee, pet food, skincare, supplements, razors. They create predictable revenue, but only if customers stay. Offer flexible control: skip, swap, pause and change frequency, because rigid subscriptions get cancelled. And follow the rules. Show the renewal price and frequency next to the sign-up button, send reminders before renewals where required, and make online cancellation easy. In the US, ROSCA and state automatic-renewal laws apply. In the UK, new subscription rules are being phased in under the DMCC Act. Trust keeps subscribers longer than friction does.
scenes.onScreen:
Subscriptions
• Best for consumables
• Skip, swap, pause, change frequency
• Renewal terms beside the button
• Easy online cancellation; US and UK rules
scenes.visual: Layout: a subscription management screen with skip, swap, pause and frequency buttons; a sign-up button with renewal terms next to it; a 'cancel online' link highlighted. Timing (39s): title 0-3s; 4 bullets build in narration order about every 8s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Referral programmes turn happy customers into acquisition channels. A classic structure: give a reward to the friend, get a reward for the referrer. Keep it easy to share on WhatsApp, Instagram and email. Pay the referrer's reward after the friend's order passes the return window. Allow one reward per new customer, and block self-referrals and obvious fraud. And measure referred customers' repeat rate, not just their first order.
scenes.onScreen:
Referral programmes
• Give X, get X
• Easy sharing on WhatsApp and social
• Reward after the return window
• One per new customer; block fraud

Timing (30s): title 0-3s; 4 bullets build in narration order about every 6s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: A simple example. A Saudi pet supplies store builds a loyalty programme around what customers value: free delivery for members, a birthday treat for their pet, points on every order, and early access to new foods. They add auto-replenishment subscriptions for pet food, with easy skip and pause. The programme costs are budgeted, and the store watches repeat purchase rate and subscription retention rather than points issued.

Simple example: Saudi pet supplies

• Pet birthday treat
• Auto-replenishment with skip/pause
• Measure repeat rate + retention

scenes.narration: Tools make this easier than it used to be. Loyalty apps like Smile dot io, LoyaltyLion and Yotpo integrate with the major ecommerce platforms. Subscription tools like Shopify Subscriptions, Recharge, Skio and Loop handle recurring orders, with skip and swap built in. In the Gulf and South Asia, loyalty status and offers increasingly travel through WhatsApp and digital wallet passes. Before choosing, check three things: whether recurring payments work with the payment methods your customers use, whether the tool supports Arabic or Urdu if you need it, and how easily you can export your data if you switch later.

scenes.narration: Now a realistic scenario with illustrative numbers. A Dubai home-fragrance brand plans give twenty dirhams, get twenty dirhams. Average order value is a hundred and eighty, gross margin fifty-five percent, and variable costs per order twenty-five. Each order contributes about seventy-four dirhams before rewards. After forty dirhams of rewards, the first order contributes about thirty-four. If referred customers place about one point two extra orders over twelve months, total contribution is around a hundred and twenty-three. The team compares that with their paid acquisition cost, and decides referrals deserve more promotion.

scenes.narration: Watch me check the referral maths. I write a small Python function with the order value, gross margin, variable cost per order, the friend's reward, the referrer's reward, and expected repeat orders in twelve months. It calculates contribution per order, subtracts both rewards from the first order, and adds contribution from repeat orders. I run it with the illustrative numbers: about thirty-four on the first order, and about a hundred and twenty-three over twelve months. Now I compare that with paid acquisition. If referrals win, I invest more. If the first order loses money and repeats are low, I switch to non-cash rewards, like early access or free delivery.

scenes.narration: Measuring loyalty impact. Compare members and non-members carefully, because loyal customers join programmes, so members always look better. Better approaches: compare repeat rates before and after launch for similar cohorts, run a holdout where a random group isn't invited, or test specific benefits. Track reward cost as a share of revenue, redemption rates, and member retention. A programme that looks amazing in a member-versus-non-member chart may be adding very little.

• Members look better by selection
• Cohorts before/after launch
• Holdouts or benefit tests
• Reward cost, redemption, retention

scenes.narration: When shouldn't you launch a loyalty programme? When the product or experience isn't good enough yet, because rewards can't fix disappointment. When purchase frequency is naturally very low, like mattresses. When margins can't support rewards. And when you don't have the resources to run it well. In those cases, focus on product quality, service and post-purchase communication first.
scenes.onScreen:
When not to launch
• Product or experience not ready
• Very low purchase frequency
• Thin margins
• No resources to run it

scenes.narration: Launching and promoting the programme matters as much as designing it. Tell customers about it at the moments they're most receptive: on the order confirmation page, in the post-purchase email, and on the packaging insert. Show members their status and progress, like you're two hundred points from twenty-five dirhams off, in emails and in their account. Make joining effortless, ideally automatic at checkout with clear consent. And train customer service to mention member benefits when they solve problems. A good programme that nobody remembers is the same as no programme at all.
scenes.onScreen:
Launch and promote
• Confirmation page, post-purchase email, packaging
• Show status and progress
• Effortless joining with consent
• Service team mentions benefits
scenes.visual: Layout: a sequence of touchpoints (order confirmation, email, parcel insert, account page) each shows a small member-progress bar filling towards a reward. Timing (40s): title 0-3s; 4 bullets build in narration order about every 8s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Common mistakes. Points nobody understands. Rewards that cost more than the behaviour they create. Rigid subscriptions that are hard to cancel. Referral rewards paid before returns clear. No fraud controls. And measuring success by members versus non-members, which flatters every programme.
scenes.onScreen:
Common mistakes
• Confusing points
• Unaffordable rewards
• Hard-to-cancel subscriptions
• Early rewards, no fraud controls
scenes.visual: Layout: red cards flip; one shows a cancel button hidden in a maze. Timing (18s): title 0-3s; 4 bullets build in narration order about every 4s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Recap. Loyalty comes from good products and experiences, and programmes amplify it. Lead with benefits customers value now, keep the maths transparent and budgeted, offer flexible subscriptions with clear renewal terms and easy cancellation, and design referral rewards that pay back with fraud controls. Measure incrementally, not with members versus non-members. Try this now: run the referral economics function from the lesson text with your own numbers, and rewrite your loyalty pitch to lead with an immediate benefit.

lessons.title: Customer experience, reviews and returns
lessons.body:
### Experience is the most powerful retention tool

Customers come back when the experience is good: accurate products, fast and reliable delivery, helpful support and easy resolution when things go wrong. Marketing can amplify a great experience but cannot compensate for a poor one.

### The post-purchase journey

```
Order confirmation   -> Clear, reassuring, with order details and support contact
Shipping updates     -> Proactive tracking; delay notifications before customers ask
Delivery             -> Packaging that protects and delights; inserts with care tips or QR codes
First use            -> How-to content; quick-start guides
Support              -> Easy channels; fast responses; empowered agents
Review request       -> Timed after the customer has used the product
Returns / exchanges  -> Simple process; clear refunds timeline
Next purchase        -> Relevant recommendations; loyalty benefits
```

### Customer service as a growth channel

- Offer channels customers use — live chat, email, phone, and messaging apps popular in your market.
- Publish response time expectations and meet them.
- Use templates for common questions, but personalise.
- Empower agents to resolve issues (refunds, replacements) within guidelines.
- Tag and analyse contact reasons monthly; fix root causes (unclear sizing, delivery delays, product defects).
- Share insights with marketing and product teams — customer questions are also content and PDP improvement ideas.

### Collecting reviews ethically

- Ask all customers (not just happy ones) after they have had time to use the product.
- Make it easy: a short form, star rating, optional photo.
- Incentives: if you offer incentives for reviews, they must not depend on the review being positive, and incentivised reviews may need to be disclosed — check local rules and platform policies.
- Never write fake reviews, pay for positive reviews, or suppress negative ones. These practices are illegal in many jurisdictions and breach marketplace and review platform policies.
- Respond to negative reviews constructively: acknowledge, explain, offer a resolution.

### Returns: reduce, then simplify

Returns are costly (shipping, handling, unsellable stock) but a fair returns policy builds trust and can increase conversion. Two-part strategy:

1. **Reduce avoidable returns**: better size guides, accurate photos and colours, detailed descriptions, fit reviews, quality control.
2. **Simplify necessary returns**: clear policy, easy process, fast refunds or exchanges, and options such as store credit.

Analyse return reasons by product. A product with a high "too small" rate may need a sizing note; one with "not as pictured" needs better photos.

Respect statutory rights: many jurisdictions give consumers cancellation rights for online purchases and rights for faulty goods, which your policy cannot remove.

### Measuring customer experience

- Customer satisfaction (CSAT) after support interactions.
- Net Promoter Score (NPS) or similar loyalty measures.
- Review ratings over time.
- Return rate by product and reason.
- First-response time and resolution time.
- Repeat purchase rate.

### Worked example: a Pakistani footwear brand

Return rate is high, mostly "wrong size". The brand adds a foot-measurement guide with a printable ruler, fit notes from reviews ("runs half a size small"), and a WhatsApp sizing assistant. It offers free exchanges for size (not refunds), and packages include a card explaining the exchange process. Returns for size fall, and customers who exchange often become repeat buyers (illustrative).

### The review rules now in force (summary)

- **US**: FTC Rule on Consumer Reviews and Testimonials (effective 21 October 2024) — no fake or AI-generated fake reviews, no buying reviews, no incentives conditioned on positive sentiment, no suppression of negative reviews, no fake "independent" review sites.
- **UK**: DMCC Act (from 6 April 2025) — fake reviews and misleading presentation of reviews are banned practices; take reasonable steps to prevent fake reviews on your site.
- **EU**: tell shoppers whether and how you check reviews are genuine.
- **Marketplaces and Google**: own policies; Google Merchant Center product ratings and seller ratings require genuine review sources.

### Hands-on: analyse return reasons and review text

Export returns (with reason codes and free-text comments) and reviews, remove personal data, then find patterns by product:

```python
import csv
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

by_product = defaultdict(Counter)
with open("returns_last_90_days.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):                  # columns: sku, reason_code, comment
        by_product[row["sku"]][row["reason_code"].strip().lower()] += 1

for sku, reasons in sorted(by_product.items(), key=lambda kv: -sum(kv[1].values()))[:10]:
    total = sum(reasons.values())
    top = ", ".join(f"{r} {n / total:.0%}" for r, n in reasons.most_common(3))
    print(f"{sku:12s} returns {total:4d}  top reasons: {top}")
```

Then read the free-text comments for the top SKUs (or have an AI assistant cluster them using a codebook, and spot-check). "Too small" suggests a sizing note; "not as pictured" suggests new photos; "damaged" points to packaging or courier issues.

### AI in customer service: guardrails

AI support agents and helpdesk AI (for example in Gorgias, Zendesk, Intercom, Freshdesk and Shopify Inbox) can answer order-status and policy questions instantly. Guardrails:

- Ground answers in **live order data and your actual policies**; never let the bot invent refund terms or delivery dates.
- Make **escalation to a human** easy, especially for complaints, vulnerable customers and payment problems.
- Tell customers when they are talking to an AI where required or expected, and log conversations for quality review.
- Measure resolution rate *and* customer satisfaction, not just deflection.

### Common mistakes

- Treating customer service as a cost centre only.
- Asking for reviews before delivery.
- Suppressing negative reviews.
- Complicated, hidden returns processes.
- Not analysing return reasons.
- Slow refunds, which generate repeat contacts, chargebacks and negative reviews.
- Treating every complaint as an isolated case instead of looking for patterns across products, couriers or regions.

### Turning feedback into improvements

Create a simple monthly loop: collect contact reasons, return reasons and review themes; rank them by frequency and cost; assign each top issue to an owner (product, marketing, operations); and track whether the issue declines after the fix. Share wins with the team — customer service staff are more engaged when they see their insights lead to change.

### Customer experience checklist

- [ ] Proactive shipping updates and delay notices
- [ ] Support channels and response times published
- [ ] Contact reasons tagged and reviewed monthly
- [ ] Ethical, timed review requests to all customers
- [ ] Return reasons analysed by product with fixes
keyTakeaways: A great experience is the strongest driver of repeat purchases.
Treat customer service insights as input for marketing and product pages.
Collect reviews from all customers ethically; never fake or suppress them.
Reduce avoidable returns first, then make necessary returns simple and fair.

options: Offering a small incentive for any honest review, disclosed where required
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Incentives must not depend on positive sentiment and may need disclosure.

options: Remove the returns policy from the website
Ground the agent in the exact policy text and live order data, add easy human escalation, and review transcripts
Let the agent decide policies case by case

scenes.narration: Here's something marketing can't fix: a disappointing experience. If the product arrives late, the size is wrong and nobody answers on WhatsApp, no email flow or loyalty programme will bring that customer back. But a great experience does the marketing for you, through repeat purchases, reviews and word of mouth. In this lecture you'll learn the post-purchase journey, customer service as a growth channel, how to collect reviews ethically under the rules now in force, how to reduce and simplify returns, how to use AI in support safely, and how to measure it all. Then you'll watch me find the story in return reasons.

Review them monthly next to your marketing metrics, because experience problems usually show up first in support and reviews, weeks before they show up in revenue.

scenes.narration: Turn feedback into improvements with a monthly loop. Gather the month's inputs: top support contact reasons, return reasons by product, new negative reviews, and satisfaction comments. Pick the three biggest themes. Share a short summary with the whole team, including marketing, so campaigns stop promising what operations can't deliver. Over a year, this simple loop does more for retention than most loyalty programmes.

lessons.title: Selling on marketplaces
lessons.body:
### Why marketplaces matter

Marketplaces — for example Amazon, noon, Daraz, eBay, Etsy and many regional platforms — bring large audiences with high purchase intent. Many shoppers start product searches on marketplaces rather than search engines. For many brands, marketplaces are a major revenue channel alongside their own store.

### Benefits and trade-offs

| Benefits | Trade-offs |
|---|---|
| Access to large, high-intent audiences | Fees (commissions, fulfilment, advertising) reduce margin |
| Trust and familiar checkout | Limited customer data and relationship ownership |
| Fulfilment services in some markets | Price competition and comparison |
| Faster market entry, including cross-border | Platform rules can change; account health risks |
| Marketplace advertising for visibility | Counterfeit and unauthorised sellers |

### Choosing marketplaces

Consider:

- Where your target customers shop (by country and category).
- Fee structures and fulfilment options.
- Category restrictions and approval requirements.
- Brand protection tools (brand registries, IP reporting).
- Operational requirements (stock, delivery times, return handling).

### Marketplace listing optimisation

Marketplaces have their own search engines. Listings should include:

- **Titles** following the marketplace's style guide, with key attributes (brand, product type, key feature, size or quantity).
- **Images** meeting requirements (for example, white-background main image where required) plus lifestyle and infographic images.
- **Bullet points** covering benefits and specifications.
- **Backend search terms** where available.
- **Enhanced brand content** (rich descriptions, comparison charts) where available.
- **Competitive pricing** and availability — both influence visibility.
- **Reviews and ratings** — collected through the marketplace's permitted methods only.

### Marketplace advertising

Most marketplaces offer sponsored product and brand ads. Principles:

- Start with your best-selling, well-reviewed products.
- Use automatic campaigns to discover search terms, then build manual campaigns around profitable terms.
- Monitor advertising cost of sales (ACoS) or return on ad spend against your margin.
- Protect branded search terms if competitors bid on them.

### Channel conflict and pricing

Selling on marketplaces and your own store can create conflict:

- Price parity: marketplaces may penalise or suppress listings priced higher than elsewhere, depending on their policies.
- Promotions: coordinate so one channel doesn't undercut another unintentionally.
- Retailer relationships: if you also sell wholesale, marketplace pricing can affect partners.

Many brands use marketplaces for acquisition and discovery while encouraging repeat purchases on their own store through packaging inserts (where marketplace rules permit), exclusive products, loyalty programmes and better service. Check each marketplace's rules on directing customers off-platform — some prohibit it.

### Worked example: a Pakistani handicrafts brand

A brand selling handmade home décor from Multan sells domestically on Daraz and internationally on Etsy, plus its own store:

- **Daraz**: price-competitive bestsellers, local delivery and cash on delivery.
- **Etsy**: unique handmade pieces, storytelling about artisans, international shipping.
- **Own store**: full collection, custom orders, and a loyalty programme; email list built from own-store customers.

Each channel's contribution margin is tracked separately after fees and shipping.

### Regional marketplace map (2026)

| Marketplace | Key markets | Notes for sellers |
|---|---|---|
| Amazon | UK (amazon.co.uk), UAE (amazon.ae), KSA (amazon.sa), US and many more | Brand Registry for brand protection and A+ content; FBA fulfilment; Amazon Ads (sponsored products, brands, display); AI shopping features such as the Rufus assistant in some markets |
| noon | UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt | Regional marketplace with its own fulfilment options and advertising; mega-sales around Ramadan, national days and White Friday |
| Daraz (Alibaba Group) | Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Myanmar | Large South Asian marketplace; COD common; big 11.11 and 12.12 campaigns; sponsored ad products |
| Etsy, eBay | International | Handmade/vintage (Etsy); broad categories (eBay) — useful for cross-border |
| TikTok Shop | Only in specific countries (see social commerce lesson) | Social marketplace with creator affiliates and live shopping |

Always check each marketplace's current seller fees, category approvals and policies — they change frequently.

### Retail media: the fastest-growing ad channel for marketplace sellers

Retail media means advertising sold by a retailer or marketplace on its own site and app (and sometimes off-site), using its shopper data. For marketplace sellers this is usually **sponsored product** and **sponsored brand** ads.

Key metrics:

```
ACoS  (advertising cost of sale)       = ad spend / ad-attributed sales
ROAS                                   = ad-attributed sales / ad spend  (= 1 / ACoS)
TACoS (total advertising cost of sale) = ad spend / TOTAL sales (ads + organic) on that marketplace
Break-even ACoS                        = contribution margin % before advertising (after marketplace fees)
```

A falling TACoS while ad spend is steady suggests ads are building organic ranking; a rising TACoS suggests you are buying sales you used to get organically.

### Hands-on: marketplace listing checklist

```
[ ] Title follows the marketplace style guide: brand + product type + key attribute + size/qty (length limits vary)
[ ] Main image meets rules (e.g. white background where required); 6+ images incl. scale, detail, in-use, infographic
[ ] 5 bullets: benefits with specs as proof; answer top objections (fit, compatibility, delivery)
[ ] Backend search terms / keywords filled where available (no competitor brands)
[ ] Arabic listing written or reviewed by a native speaker for amazon.ae/.sa and noon
[ ] Price competitive and consistent with your policies; stock synced to avoid cancellations
[ ] Brand registry / IP protection enrolled; counterfeit reporting process known
[ ] Reviews only through permitted programmes (e.g. Amazon Vine) - no off-platform incentives
```

### Common mistakes

- Treating marketplace revenue as profit without subtracting fees and advertising.
- Poor listings (few images, weak titles).
- Ignoring account health metrics (late shipments, cancellations, policy violations).
- Breaking marketplace rules on reviews or off-platform contact.
- No brand protection against counterfeits.
- Letting stock run out on marketplace bestsellers, which can hurt ranking long after stock returns.

### Starting small

If you are new to marketplaces, start with a limited range of your best-selling, well-reviewed products that have healthy margins after fees. Learn the platform's fulfilment, advertising and account health requirements before expanding. Track each product's contribution margin after commission, fulfilment, advertising and returns; some products that are profitable on your own store will not be profitable on a marketplace, and that is fine — sell them where they work.

### Cross-border marketplace selling

Marketplaces can help you reach other countries, but consider duties and taxes, product regulations and labelling, delivery times and costs, returns handling across borders, and local language listings. Pilot in one new market before expanding further.

### Marketplace checklist

- [ ] Marketplace selection based on customers and economics
- [ ] Listings optimised to each marketplace's guidelines
- [ ] Contribution margin tracked per channel after all fees
- [ ] Advertising measured against margin
- [ ] Brand protection and account health monitored
keyTakeaways: Marketplaces offer high-intent audiences but reduce margin and customer ownership.
Optimise listings for each marketplace's search and style rules.
Track contribution margin per channel after fees and advertising.
Follow marketplace rules on reviews, pricing and off-platform contact.

lessons.title: Social commerce and creator-led selling
lessons.body:
### Shopping where attention lives

**Social commerce** means selling directly within or via social platforms — shoppable posts, in-app shops, live shopping, and creator-led sales. It shortens the path from inspiration to purchase.

### Social commerce options (availability varies by country)

| Option | Description |
|---|---|
| Shoppable posts and product tags | Tag products in posts and videos, linking to product details |
| In-app shops | Storefronts inside social apps; checkout may happen in-app or on your site |
| Social marketplaces | Platform shops with integrated fulfilment in some markets |
| Live shopping | Real-time selling with demonstrations and Q&A |
| Messaging commerce | Catalogues and ordering via messaging apps (common in the Gulf and South Asia) |
| Creator affiliate programmes | Creators earn commission on sales through their content |

Features and availability change often and differ by country — check each platform's current commerce offering in your markets.

### What sells on social

- Products with **visual appeal** or demonstrable results (beauty, fashion, gadgets, home).
- **Impulse-friendly price points**.
- Products that benefit from **explanation or demonstration**.
- **Trending** or novel items.
- Brands with **community and personality**.

### Content that converts on social

- **Demonstrations**: show the product solving a problem.
- **Before and after** (only if genuine and compliant with platform rules and advertising codes — restricted in some categories).
- **Creator reviews and tutorials** (disclosed).
- **Unboxing and first impressions**.
- **Behind the scenes**: how products are made.
- **Live Q&A** answering objections in real time.

### Messaging commerce

In markets where messaging apps dominate, many stores sell through conversations: customers ask questions, receive catalogue links, and confirm orders in chat. To scale this responsibly:

- Use business accounts with catalogues and quick replies.
- Respond quickly with clear information (price, delivery, payment options).
- Confirm orders in writing, including delivery date and total cost.
- Collect marketing opt-in explicitly before sending promotional messages.
- Keep customer data secure.

### Live shopping

Live shopping combines entertainment and selling. Tips:

- Plan a run-sheet: products, demos, offers, questions to address.
- Have a host who knows the products and a moderator for comments.
- Offer genuine live-only incentives if appropriate (with clear terms).
- Repurpose the recording into short clips.

### Measuring social commerce

Track: sales attributed to social shops and links, conversion rate, AOV, return rate (social impulse purchases can have higher returns), customer acquisition cost, and repeat purchase rate of social-acquired customers. Compare with other channels on contribution margin.

### Worked example: a Dubai beauty brand

The brand runs weekly live sessions demonstrating products for different skin types, with a creator co-host (paid partnership, disclosed). Shoppable clips from each live are posted during the week. Customers can also order via a messaging app catalogue. The team discovers that live-session buyers have higher AOV but also higher return rates for shade-matching issues, so it adds a shade-finder quiz and offers shade samples.

### Where TikTok Shop and in-app shopping actually operate

Availability changes often and differs by country. As of mid-2026, TikTok Shop's local seller programme operated in a specific list of markets that included the **US, Mexico and Brazil; Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines, Singapore and Japan; and the UK, Ireland and a growing set of EU countries** (including Germany, France, Italy and Spain, with further EU markets added in 2026). It was **not** available for local sellers in Pakistan, the UAE or Saudi Arabia at that time. Always check TikTok Shop's official seller site for your market before planning.

Other options:
- **Instagram and Facebook product tagging** (shoppable posts linking to your site; in-app checkout availability varies by market).
- **YouTube Shopping** product tagging and affiliate programmes in eligible countries.
- **Snapchat** is heavily used in Saudi Arabia; shoppable ads and catalogues can suit Gulf brands.
- **WhatsApp Business catalogues** and conversational ordering (Gulf, Pakistan).

### Hands-on: a live shopping run-sheet

```
Title:     "Summer skincare for oily skin - live Q&A" (45 min)
Host:      brand educator; co-host creator (paid partnership, disclosed on screen + platform label)
Moderator: answers comments, pins product links, flags questions for the host
00:00-03:00  Hook + what viewers will learn; disclosure; live-only offer terms on screen
03:00-15:00  Product 1 demo: texture close-up, how to layer, skin-type suitability
15:00-25:00  Product 2 demo + top 3 questions from comments
25:00-35:00  Viewer questions; shade/skin-type guidance; delivery dates by city
35:00-42:00  Bundle recap; offer ends when stream ends (genuine)
42:00-45:00  Thank you; where to find the replay; customer service contact
After:       Clip 5-8 short videos; tag products; log questions for FAQ and PDP updates
Metrics:     viewers, peak concurrent, product clicks, orders, AOV, return rate (next 30 days)
```

### Measuring social commerce honestly

Social-driven purchases can have higher return rates (impulse buys, shade/size mismatch). Track contribution margin **after returns** by channel, and compare repeat purchase rates of social-acquired customers with other channels before scaling.

### Common mistakes

- Assuming social commerce features are available in every market.
- Ignoring returns and margin in social-driven sales.
- Undisclosed creator partnerships.
- Slow responses in messaging commerce.
- Sending promotional messages without opt-in.
- Measuring only views and likes rather than orders, margin and repeat purchases.

### Operations behind social selling

Social selling can create sudden demand spikes when content performs well. Prepare by keeping stock buffers for featured products, having customer service ready for message volumes, and making sure delivery promises in content are realistic. Record which pieces of content drove sales so you can brief creators and plan future lives with evidence.

### Building community around social commerce

The strongest social commerce brands treat followers as a community, not just an audience: they reply to comments, feature customers (with permission), ask for product ideas, and reward loyal followers with early access. Community turns one-off impulse buyers into repeat customers and advocates.

### Social commerce checklist

- [ ] Platform features confirmed for your markets
- [ ] Content plan built around demonstrations and creators
- [ ] Messaging commerce with fast responses and written confirmations
- [ ] Disclosures for all paid partnerships
- [ ] Contribution margin and returns tracked for social sales

lessons.title: Google Merchant Center and product feeds
lessons.body:
### Why the product feed is now your most important ad asset

A **product feed** is a structured list of your products — IDs, titles, descriptions, prices, availability, images, identifiers and more. Google Merchant Center uses it for **free listings** on Google (Shopping tab, Search, Images, Maps/YouTube in eligible markets) and for **Shopping ads and Performance Max**. The same data powers Meta and TikTok catalogues, marketplaces and increasingly AI shopping experiences. A clean, rich feed improves visibility everywhere; a messy one quietly limits every channel.

### Required and key attributes (Google Merchant Center)

| Attribute | Notes |
|---|---|
| `id` | Unique, stable per variant (e.g. SKU). Changing IDs resets performance history. |
| `title` | Up to 150 characters. Front-load what shoppers search: brand + product type + key attributes (material, size, colour, gender, model). |
| `description` | Up to 5,000 characters; accurate, no promotional text or competitor comparisons. |
| `link` | Landing page for the exact variant; must match the feed price and availability. |
| `image_link` | High-quality image of the product; no watermarks or promotional overlays on the main image. |
| `availability` | `in_stock`, `out_of_stock`, `preorder`, `backorder`. |
| `price` | Number + ISO currency, e.g. `189.00 AED`; must match the landing page. |
| `brand` | Required for most new products with a brand. |
| `gtin` | Required when the product has one assigned (EAN/UPC/ISBN). Use `mpn` + `brand` if no GTIN; `identifier_exists = no` only when neither exists (e.g. custom-made). |
| `condition` | `new`, `refurbished` or `used`. |
| Variant attributes | `item_group_id`, `color`, `size`, `gender`, `age_group` (required for apparel in many countries). |
| `shipping` / `tax` | Shipping cost and speed settings (account-level or in feed); tax settings in some countries (e.g. US). |
| Optional but valuable | `sale_price` + `sale_price_effective_date`, `product_highlight`, `product_detail`, `additional_image_link`, `custom_label_0-4`, `google_product_category`, `product_type`. |

Always check the current *Product data specification* in Merchant Center Help — requirements differ by country and category and change over time.

### Ways to submit and manage the feed

- **Platform integrations**: Shopify's Google & YouTube channel app, WooCommerce's Google for WooCommerce extension, and marketplace-style connectors sync products automatically.
- **Scheduled file fetch** (CSV/TSV/XML hosted on your server) or **Google Sheets**.
- **API**: the **Merchant API** replaced the Content API for Shopping, which was scheduled to shut down on 18 August 2026. If a developer or feed tool integrated with the Content API, confirm it has migrated. File uploads, scheduled fetches and Sheets are not affected.
- **Supplemental feeds** add or override attributes (custom labels, better titles) without touching the primary feed.
- **Feed management tools** (e.g. Feedonomics, Channable, Productsup, DataFeedWatch) help at scale and across channels.

### Hands-on: validate a feed before Google does

```python
import csv

REQUIRED = ["id", "title", "description", "link", "image_link", "availability", "price", "brand", "condition"]
AVAILABILITY = {"in_stock", "out_of_stock", "preorder", "backorder"}
CONDITION = {"new", "refurbished", "used"}

def gtin_ok(gtin: str) -> bool:
    """GS1 check digit for GTIN-8/12/13/14."""
    if not gtin.isdigit() or len(gtin) not in (8, 12, 13, 14):
        return False
    digits = [int(d) for d in gtin]
    check = digits.pop()
    total = sum(d * (3 if i % 2 == 0 else 1) for i, d in enumerate(reversed(digits)))
    return (10 - total % 10) % 10 == check

problems = 0
with open("products.tsv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for n, row in enumerate(csv.DictReader(f, delimiter="\t"), start=2):
        issues = [f"missing {k}" for k in REQUIRED if not (row.get(k) or "").strip()]
        if len(row.get("title", "")) > 150: issues.append("title > 150 chars")
        if row.get("availability") and row["availability"] not in AVAILABILITY: issues.append("bad availability value")
        if row.get("condition") and row["condition"] not in CONDITION: issues.append("bad condition value")
        if len((row.get("price") or "").split()) != 2: issues.append("price should be like '189.00 AED'")
        gtin = (row.get("gtin") or "").strip()
        if gtin and not gtin_ok(gtin): issues.append(f"gtin {gtin} fails check digit")
        for i in issues:
            problems += 1
            print(f"line {n} id={row.get('id', '?')}: {i}")
print(f"{problems} problem(s) found")
```

Example TSV (header + one row):

```text
id	title	description	link	image_link	availability	price	brand	gtin	condition	item_group_id	color	size	custom_label_0
LNS-SAND-M	ExampleBrand Linen Relaxed Shirt - Sand - Men's M	Breathable 100% linen shirt, relaxed fit.	https://example.com/p/linen-sand?variant=m	https://example.com/i/linen-sand-1.jpg	in_stock	189.00 AED	ExampleBrand	5012345678900	new	LNS-SAND	Sand	M	margin_high
```

### Common disapprovals and how to avoid them

| Issue | Typical cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Price mismatch | Feed not updated after a sale; currency/tax display differs | Sync prices automatically; use `sale_price` with effective dates |
| Availability mismatch | Stock changes faster than feed updates | More frequent syncs; structured data on the page matching the feed |
| Missing identifiers | No GTIN/brand/MPN | Add GS1 GTINs; `identifier_exists` only when truly none |
| Misrepresentation (account level) | Unclear business identity, missing policies, misleading claims | Clear contact details, returns/delivery policies, honest pricing and claims |
| Image problems | Watermarks, promo text, placeholder images | Clean main images; lifestyle images as additional images |

### Free listings, promotions and ratings

- **Free listings** can bring clicks at no cost once the feed is approved — a strong reason for every store to use Merchant Center, even without ads.
- **Promotions** (e.g. "10% off with code EID10") can appear on listings; terms must match your site and pass review.
- **Product ratings** and **store ratings** can show when you have enough genuine reviews from supported sources.
- **Local inventory** features let stores with physical locations show in-store availability.

### AI and the feed

Merchant Center includes AI tools (for example Product Studio for image editing and generation, and suggested title/description improvements). Use them to improve imagery and fill gaps, but check accuracy: AI-generated backgrounds are fine; AI changes to the product itself (colour, shape, included items) are misleading. Remember that AI shopping experiences — Google's and others' — read your structured product data, so accurate, complete attributes help you appear for detailed queries like "breathable linen shirt for 40°C".
